extracted.subtask_short: writing news reports on fires and accidents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplar copy for reporting fires, accidents, shipwrecks, mine explosions and other casualty stories — focusing on selection, arrangement, factual detail, eyewitness material and human-interest context. Uses multiple newspaper versions of the same incidents as teaching examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare different arrangements of same material
rubrics_metrics.description: The same event can be arranged and written in different ways; students should compare multiple newspaper accounts of the same accident to see how selection and ordering change emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note in the text: "The following ... should be compared as reports of the same accident given in two New York morning papers." Use paired versions of an incident to study arrangement, lead focus, and what facts are included or omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a clear factual lead (who/what/when/where/why/how)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with the essential facts of the incident — location, time, what happened, and immediate consequences — so the reader quickly understands the core news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the samples: leads giving city, date and succinct statement of disaster (e.g., 'JERSEY CITY, N. J., Nov. 6.— Four were killed and over 200 were injured in the wreck...'). The lead may also note outstanding facts (number dead/injured) or an unusual causal point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include precise identifying details of victims and injured
rubrics_metrics.description: When available, list the names, ages, hometowns/addresses, and occupations of the dead and injured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Jersey City report includes a named list headed 'The following are the dead:' and a hospital-made list of injured giving names, ages and towns. Such specifics lend authority and human concreteness to reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report official findings and investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Include statements about causes, findings of official inquiries, or ongoing investigations (broken rail, arrested personnel, coroner inquiries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: police found a broken rail and agreed it was cause; towerman Williamson was arrested and discharged; officials investigating cause of wreck. Attribute these claims to the investigating authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide timeline and operational/logistical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain sequence and logistics: scheduled times, delays, relief/rescue train dispatches, how long wrecking/cleanup took, and times when help arrived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: train due in Milwaukee at 12:10 a.m., brought in by relief train at 4 a.m.; wrecker did not get out until 4 a.m. These details help readers understand scale and response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid descriptive details to convey the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ concrete visual and physical details (distances, structural damage, motions, weather effects) to make the incident comprehensible and immediate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated throughout: 'tore along for over 150 yards, across a trestle', 'engine toppled over, part of it lying across the trestle work', 'stem lifting so high... twenty feet of the keel visible'. Such description should support, not substitute for, facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate eyewitness and survivor accounts/quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Include first-person accounts, quotations and recollections from survivors, rescuers, or on-scene officials to add immediacy and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: survivor Farrell's narrative of the Leggett sinking; Diver Jack Hanson's quoted line about rescuing the men. Attribute and, where necessary, corroborate eyewitness details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note material, property and cargo details when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Report on significant property losses, cargo particulars, or valuables involved (mail car specie, ship cargo, tonnage) as they affect the story's impact and possible follow-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'In the mail car ... was more than $1,000,000 in specie' and detailed cargo lists for ships. Give concrete quantities and likely consequences when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute and quote officials, experts and rescuers
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite statements from captains, superintendents, mine inspectors, coroners and other authorities to explain decisions, responsibility, or technical causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: State Mine Inspector Louttit and Mine Foreman Kennedy examining the mine; Captain Brown's account of holding the steamer's bow. Proper attribution increases credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include technical/specification background when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide technical specs and background (ship tonnage, dimensions, construction notes) that help explain why events unfolded as they did or their significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Alma E. A. Holmes' gross register, length, beam, build year; Leggett's gross tonnage and cargo capacity. Use such details sparingly and only when they illuminate the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add biographical/contextual details for notable victims
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prominent person is involved, include concise biographical context to explain their public significance and augment reader interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Spencer Trask's background (financier, association with Edison, director of railroads, bought and reorganized The New York Times, club memberships, marriage) accompanies the death notice to contextualize impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe rescue/recovery efforts and human-interest elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Report how rescue teams, medical personnel, or communities responded, including difficulties, heroism, public reaction, and relief measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: detailed rescue activity (ambulances, police patrols, fire wagons used to remove injured), townspeople crowding the mine shaft, divers' rescue attempts, funds raised for work crews. These elements add narrative and social context.
